results.construction: On the 6x6 grid select the six cells with first+second=7: (1,6),(2,5),(3,4),(4,3),(5,2),(6,1). n(E)=6, n(S)=36, P=6/36=1/6. Within limits (rows, cols 2-8; event nonempty).

predicates.why: A student who treats 'total 7' as a single outcome would select one cell (or one representative), so the grid shows one way where six exist. This is the misconception's signature build.

It fires for any incomplete selection, e.g. a student who treats (1,6) and (6,1) as the same and picks only three cells, or who just overlooks the diagonal. Those are order errors or carelessness, not the compound-outcome-counted-once misconception, so this predicate would mostly fire for other reasons.

results.construction: Spec {"rows":6,"cols":6,"rule":{"kind":"sum","op":"eq","value":5}}. Select cells (1,4),(2,3),(3,2),(4,1). n(E)=4, n(S)=36, P=4/36=1/9. Within 6x6 limits, event non-empty.

predicates.why: A student who treats 'total of 5' as a single outcome selects one cell (or one per unordered pair), collapsing the several ordered ways into one. That is exactly this misconception, and the grid shows 4 ways.

It fires for any omitted cell, including slips, losing track while dragging, or forgetting reversed pairs. Those are not specific to the compound-outcome-counted-once belief, so it would mostly fire for other reasons and the diagnosis would be unjustified.

results.construction: Grid 6x6, rule {kind:sum, op:eq, value:9}. Select cells (3,6),(4,5),(5,4),(6,3); n(E)=4, n(S)=36, P=4/36=1/9.

predicates.why: A student who treats 'total 9' as a single outcome selects one cell, or one per unordered pair, instead of all four ordered pairs. That is the compound-outcome-counted-once error, so the predicate fits.
It fires for any incomplete selection, such as forgetting a mirrored pair or a slip. That is mostly not the compound-outcome-counted-once misconception, so the diagnosis is too generic.
